question: True or false: if a man chose to set off too late to keep a promise, most say he no longer ought to keep it?
answer: False. In Chituc and colleagues' 2016 experiments, most people said he still ought to meet his friend, though he no longer could. When a breakdown he was not to blame for stopped him, fewer said so. Their verdicts tracked blame, not ability: the old maxim that ought implies can fitted only the blameless.
move: Before naming the cause, check what else always comes with it.
trap: Crediting inability, which in everyday cases arrives together with blamelessness.
reference: Chituc, Henne, Sinnott-Armstrong & De Brigard, Blame, not ability, impacts moral 'ought' judgments for impossible actions, Cognition 150, 2016, pp. 20-25
